html:
The Holy Roman Empire was a loose union of hundreds of kingdoms, duchies, bishoprics and free cities in central Europe, headed by an elected emperor, which lasted from 962 to 1806. It covered roughly modern Germany, Austria, the Czech lands and, at times, the Low Countries and northern Italy.

Its roots lay in the eastern part of the Frankish realm and in Charlemagne's imperial title of 800. The chart starts it in 962, when the German king Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome. The emperors claimed to continue the Roman Empire and to protect the Church, and that claim led to long fights with the popes, above all the Investiture Controversy over who appointed bishops.

How it worked:

  • The emperor was chosen by a small group of princes, the electors, fixed at seven by the Golden Bull of 1356.
  • Princes ran their own lands; the emperor ruled mainly through his own family's holdings.
  • From 1438 the Habsburgs of Austria held the title almost without a break.

Charles V, who also ruled Spain, faced Martin Luther and the Reformation, which split the empire between Catholic and Protestant princes. The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) devastated it, and the Peace of Westphalia left the princes nearly sovereign.

Voltaire joked that it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. Yet it kept the peace among its many small states for long stretches. Napoleon reorganised Germany, and Francis II dissolved the empire in 1806. Its lands later became the cores of Germany and Austria.
